entries.description: Run several accounts of one provider in Duckwork' credential pool: `duckwork account <provider> <action>` adds accounts with email verification, shows live usage per account, keeps the least-used account first (fill_first + a 5-minute balance timer over every provider with accounts), parks accounts for hours or on a weekly schedule, shows which bot is on which account and its tokens at API prices, alerts on dead logins, a full pool or a runaway bot, and can start an idle account's 5-hour window with one tiny request (wake). Adapters for anthropic and openai-codex; generic commands for any pool provider. Optional Accounts page in Duckwork Desktop. Linux and Windows. Disclosure — logins stay in Duckwork: park holds an entry out of rotation in Duckwork' pool (mark_exhausted_and_rotate, reason "parked") and unpark is reset_status; the plugin's park list holds labels, ids and times only; expired tokens are refreshed by Duckwork (try_refresh_matching); sign-in, in the terminal and on the Desktop page, runs `duckwork auth add`; other profiles' accounts are read with read_credential_pool. It uses each account's access token as Duckwork stores it for live usage and the email check (api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/usage and /profile, chatgpt.com/backend-api/wham/usage, with the client headers of Duckwork' usage fetcher) and for wake (a command, a page button, or the timer after the opt-in `wake auto-on`): one one-word request per account through Duckwork' Anthropic client or the Codex Responses endpoint, and the account's model list. Telegram alerts through `duckwork send -t telegram` to the bot's home channel or a chat id kept in account-pool.json; no telemetry. Its session tracker, a post_api_request hook, runs in every profile and writes labels, ids and token counts only. `setup` writes plugins.enabled of every profile, links the plugin into every profile, removes the retired account-pool-tracker (`duckwork plugins remove`) and, with --timer, adds a systemd user timer (Linux) or a Task Scheduler task for the user (Windows, no admin rights). Runs systemctl --user and notify-send (Linux), schtasks, powershell.exe and taskkill (Windows), duckwork config set, duckwork auth add/remove, duckwork send, duckwork plugins remove; reads every profile's config.yaml and state.db (read-only), the gateway config (whether the Telegram bot has a home channel) and /proc on Linux. The command registers in the default profile only and provides no tools. Live usage, the email check and wake send each account's own access token from Duckwork' pool straight to its vendor with Claude Code (anthropic) and Codex CLI (openai-codex) client headers. The session tracker reads the running agent's current pool account (label and id only) by scanning Python thread frames for Duckwork' private _credential_pool. On the first run after 3.x it moves parked logins from account-pool-parked.json back into Duckwork' pool and deletes that file.
known_issues: After installing, run `duckwork account <provider> setup` (add --timer for the 5-minute balance timer): it lists the plugin in every profile for the Desktop page and links it into every profile for the session tracker. Coming from 3.x it also removes account-pool-tracker.

Duckwork can let a parked account back into rotation early (`duckwork auth reset`, or a Codex quota it sees come back); the next balance run parks it again, and doctor names it until then. A park without --until is held for 30 days, and a balance run renews it once less than 15 days are left, so without the timer it ends after 30 days.

Windows: tested with a stand-in Task Scheduler and, up to 3.13, with Windows' own Python, cmd.exe and wscript.exe under Wine; not yet on a Windows machine. On Windows the timer runs only while the user is signed in.
Built for plugins.isolation: in_process (the default). Under host, Duckwork skips plugin CLI commands, so `duckwork account` and the timer's balance are unavailable.

Usage comes from undocumented provider endpoints (api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/usage, chatgpt.com/backend-api/wham/usage) that can change or rate-limit without notice; bots are unaffected when they do.

The Desktop page's sign-in relays `duckwork auth add` and has run in sandbox tests (Duckwork' real sign-in code, provider calls replaced), not yet with a new account on a real install. The Codex browser sign-in needs the browser on the same computer; when port 1455 is taken, Duckwork signs in with a device code instead.
entries.name: account-pool
entries.title: Account Pool

entries.description: Windows desktop plugin that switches which Codex login and which Claude subscription account every local Duckwork profile uses, with one idle-only, verified restart of the gateway (and, on Duckwork before 0.22, of Duckwork Desktop). Refuses while any profile is busy, restores the previous selection if a step fails, and writes a receipt that says whether the switch took effect. Disclosure — Windows only. A switch rewrites, through Duckwork's own commands, the Codex credential order in every profile's auth.json and the CLAUDE_SUBSCRIPTION_DIRECTSDK_CONFIG_DIR line in every profile's .env, so every profile that has the plugin enabled spends the same selected Codex login and the same Claude login (one Duckwork-owned claude-auth folder; no token is copied between profiles). It reads Codex tokens from each profile's auth.json. On Duckwork 0.22 and later it stops and restarts the gateway once Duckwork's own idle proof and the gateway's drain report idle, and Duckwork Desktop stays open and reconnects; on earlier Duckwork it also reads the Desktop backends' dashboard session token from their process environment and closes and reopens Duckwork Desktop (work started in the seconds after the idle check is cut off). It sends the target Codex token to OpenAI's usage endpoint and Claude login tokens to Anthropic's OAuth profile endpoint (also when the setup screen opens); if the target Claude login has expired it first runs the claude CLI once so the CLI renews its own token, which rotates that login's refresh token. No telemetry and no automatic account rotation.

entries.description: Make Duckwork a team member in an ActVox workspace: on a schedule it works the tasks people assign it and answers the comments that @mention it, and submits each task for a person's review. Skills actvox:actvox and actvox:actvox-inbox, a first-turn inbox line (pre_llm_call), /actvox inbox|status, and duckwork actvox setup|install-gate. A cron pre-run gate wakes the agent only when the inbox has work, so an empty tick makes no model call. Disclosure — ActVox is reached only through the user's own actvox MCP server (ctx.call_mcp, needs plugins.entries.actvox.mcp_allowlist) and the user's own actvox CLI (the gate runs `actvox inbox --all --json`); on the first turn of every non-cron session the pre_llm_call hook calls the server's check_inbox (up to 5 s) and adds one line saying how many tasks and mentions wait; the plugin holds and reads no credential and sends no telemetry. `duckwork actvox install-gate` writes one file, $DUCKWORK_HOME/scripts/actvox-inbox-gate.py, only on that explicit command and never over a file it did not write; gate state lives in $DUCKWORK_HOME/plugin-data/actvox/. No background work of its own: the cron job runs only after the user creates it, and from then on anyone who can assign Duckwork a task or @mention it in your ActVox workspaces decides what an unattended agent run on your host works on, with that job's toolsets (dangerous commands follow approvals.cron_mode, deny by default). Unattended writes need the default trust: full on the actvox server.

entries.description: Two extra delegation modes for `delegate_task`, next to the built-in default. Model routes (`delegation.backend: model_map`): the agent picks a named model route per subagent from a list you define (e.g. fast, deep, local). Profile routes (`delegation.backend: profile_routes`): the agent runs a subagent as one of your Duckwork profiles, with that profile's own model, credentials, skills and SOUL.md. Only route names and their one-line descriptions reach the model. Adds `duckwork delegation config` (pick the mode and edit its routes; `--show` prints the setup) and the `/delegation` slash command (save a mode for the next session, or `--now` to apply it to the current chat). Needs Duckwork 0.22.5 or newer, the first release with pluggable delegation providers; Duckwork 0.22.0 to 0.22.4 refuses to install it, and on a core older than 0.22.0 it installs, logs one warning and does nothing. Disclosure — no Python dependencies and no network or model calls of its own; subagents run through core's `delegate_task` on the routes you configured. Writes only `delegation.backend` and `delegation.backends.*` (model_map / profile_routes) in the active profile's config.yaml, through core's config writer. A model route's optional `api_key` is stored in config.yaml in plain text (`provider:` keeps keys in .env / auth.json). Listing a profile under profile routes lets this profile's subagents use that profile's credentials, SOUL.md and terminal policy.

entries.title: Advanced Delegation

entries.description: A persistent second model reviews every agent turn. After each turn the plugin hands the transcript to the model you nominate as advisor and delivers its findings as advice in the same session: [NIT], [CONCERN] or [BLOCKER] notes, held back until a later review raises the same point again, so the primary agent is not interrupted by a one-off remark. It reviews, it does not act: the advisor never edits files, calls tools or changes session state, and only reads the turn transcript. This is the backend counterpart of MoA — one extra model, not a committee: the primary agent does the work and the advisor checks it. Port of pi-omplike-advisor (Petr Baudis / pasky), itself rooted in oh-my-pi (Can Boluk). Runs inside the plugin host with no dependencies beyond Duckwork itself. Disclosure — once the plugin is enabled, every completed turn costs one extra completion through Duckwork's ctx.llm to the advisor model (the primary agent's provider unless you allow a provider/model override under plugins.entries.advisor.llm), carrying the user message, the final reply, every tool call and tool result in the session so far (each clipped to 500 characters) and the contents of a WATCHDOG.md in Duckwork's working directory if one exists; deliverable advice is queued into the CLI session as a user-role message, which starts or interrupts an agent turn; state is kept under $DUCKWORK_HOME/advisor/ and reviews run on one background thread; no other network, files or credentials.
known_issues: Every reviewed turn costs one extra completion on the advisor model. Reviews run on a single worker in the background after the hook returns (the hook itself never blocks turn finalization), so a long advisor call delays advice, not the agent.

Advice is injected into the live conversation with ctx.inject_message, which the interactive CLI provides. On gateway surfaces (Telegram, Slack, ...) the review still runs and its notes are held, but there is no in-session place to inject them, so delivery is CLI-shaped.

Concerns are only delivered once a later review repeats them (hold-and-reconfirm), so a genuine one-off concern can stay silent by design. /advisor test <severity> <note> injects a synthetic note to see the delivery path.
The cross-provider trust gate is conservative: point the advisor at a provider different from the primary agent's, or accept the default inherit-primary behaviour.

The interactive provider/model picker (/advisor model with no argument) needs PluginContext.request_model_selection, and the status-bar badge needs ctx.register_status_segment. Where a build lacks those newer seams the plugin still loads and the text commands keep working (/advisor provider <name>, /advisor model <name>).
State lives in $DUCKWORK_HOME/advisor/state.json, per profile.
entries.name: advisor
entries.title: Advisor

entries.description: Parallel AI task orchestrator. Paste a task list into the desktop panel; Duckwork phases it into dependency-ordered groups through the agent_batch_plan / agent_batch_phase tools (or you group it yourself in one click), then each phase dispatches one independent coding agent per task to a GitHub Actions workflow in a repo you name — own branch, own PR — and the panel tracks the runs and the PRs. GITHUB_TOKEN is the only required credential; AGENT_BATCH_REPO, AGENT_BATCH_WORKFLOW, AGENT_BATCH_MODEL and AGENT_BATCH_STATE are optional (the last is a directory override for the plan file, not a secret) and each can be set per plan in the panel instead. Disclosure — Duckwork can read and rewrite the stored phase plan through the agent_batch_plan / agent_batch_phase tools, but dispatch is always a confirmed click in the panel. Each dispatch fires a GitHub workflow_dispatch with your GITHUB_TOKEN (Actions + pull-requests write) on the repo you name. The workflow you copy into that repo installs third-party coding-agent CLIs (cline by default; the others are unpinned npm packages) and runs them unattended, with auto-approve / skip-permissions, repo write access and your provider secrets. They push real branches and open real PRs, and your task text and repository code go to that runner's model vendor. LLM cost belongs to the runner: cline spends Cline Credits or a BYOK key, opencode free models need its zen relay, kilo needs an active Kilo Go subscription (keyless CI runs fail), and claude-code / codex / dsh need their own keys.

entries.description: Give the inference engine behind each request a standard, machine-readable view of the agent session that produced it. Injects an X-Agent-Hint header (base64url JSON: session identity and call index, lifecycle state, soft priority, a cache-pinning hint, optional measured statistics) on main LLM requests, and can emit session lifecycle events out of band as local ndjson or as POSTs to a URL you configure. Request bodies are never modified, and nothing is added or sent until the plugin is enabled. Lets a scheduler pin a session to the instance already holding its KV cache, or rank a user-blocked session above background work, without teaching the engine anything about the client. Disclosure — when enabled, every main LLM request carries an X-Agent-Hint header (base64url JSON with the session id, call index, lifecycle state, priority and cache hints) to whatever provider is configured, not only hint-aware engines; with status_sink: http the same session events and usage/latency statistics are POSTed to the status_url you set, and ndjson writes them under $DUCKWORK_HOME.
entries.name: agent-hint

entries.description: `duckwork import-agent`: import an OpenClaw (~/.openclaw, or legacy ~/.clawdbot / ~/.moltbot), Claude Code (~/.claude), Codex CLI (~/.codex) or Cursor (~/.cursor) setup into Duckwork in one command; always previews first and asks before applying. Claude Code / Codex / Cursor: instructions, Cursor rules and memories become memory entries, Bash permission rules become command allow/deny lists, MCP servers land in config.yaml, skills are copied, and `--sync` re-imports sources that changed. OpenClaw (core's former `duckwork claw migrate`; the plugin keeps that spelling, `duckwork claw cleanup` and the openclaw-migration skill): persona, memories, skills, model and messaging settings, MCP servers and agent behaviour. Formerly built into Duckwork core; `duckwork setup` offers to install it when it finds one of these agents, and profiles with a registered sync source are migrated automatically. Disclosure — no Python dependencies, no network calls and no model calls. Claude Code / Codex / Cursor: reads those agents' local config trees (never their credential files; secret-looking MCP env vars and headers are stripped and listed) and writes only into the active profile (memories/MEMORY.md with a backup, config.yaml, skills/ and import-sync.json). OpenClaw: reads the OpenClaw dir (openclaw.json, its .env, workspace files such as SOUL.md / MEMORY.md / USER.md, skills); API keys and bot tokens come over only with --migrate-secrets (allowlisted names, shown in the preview). It writes into the active profile (config.yaml, .env, SOUL.md, memories/, skills/openclaw-imports/, a migration/openclaw/<time>/ report with item backups, and a backups/pre-migration-*.zip restore point), plus a workspace dir only when --workspace-target names one. It runs local pgrep / systemctl / tasklist checks to warn when OpenClaw or a Duckwork gateway is still running, and `duckwork claw cleanup` renames the OpenClaw dir to *.pre-migration after a confirmation.
entries.name: agent-importers

entries.description: Process hygiene for agent machines — finds the background processes your agent left behind (dev servers, tunnels, watchers, nohup jobs) using evidence signals (ppid=1 reparent, port listener via /proc/net/tcp{,6}, dev-server traits, TTL exceeded) and attributes them to the originating tool call via agent-ledger's ledger when present. Dry-run by default: nothing is killed until you write policy_mode=enforce; system daemons and host/VM management agents are exempt by name, a user-editable whitelist covers your real infrastructure, and each kill re-reads the cmdline first (SIGTERM, 2s, SIGKILL with PID-reuse check). stdlib-only, fails open. Disclosure — inside Duckwork it only appends terminal commands that look like they start background work (first 300 characters, which can include inline secrets) to plugin-data/agent-janitor/spawns.jsonl, and reads agent-ledger's ledger.db read-only when present. Killing is a separate CLI you run yourself (janitor_cli.py sweep): after you write "enforce" to plugin-data/agent-janitor/policy_mode it sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL to every process re-parented to PID 1 for over a minute that is not on its built-in exempt list or your whitelist, whoever started it (for example a tmux server or a nohup'd duckwork gateway), including other users' processes when run as root. Dry-run first; the dry-run list is the kill list.
entries.name: agent-janitor

entries.description: Write-ahead ledger for agent side effects, with an OWASP Agentic Top 10 posture scorer. entries.description: Self-driving multi-agent development team. Role-based workers (architect, developer, reviewer, tester, researcher, writer, devops) are each a real Duckwork profile with its own SOUL.md and skills; they discuss and vote on decisions, and the adopted conclusion is executed by the same team. A "leader" profile chairs the discussions and a heartbeat cron wakes it to assess state, unblock workers and plan the next phase. Discussion and execution share one board: a motion is a sub-task of a per-project team channel task, speech and votes are `[agora:msg]` comments, the conclusion is written to task.result, and an adopted conclusion becomes execution tasks parented to the motion so context reaches workers through Duckwork' own parent handoff. Ships 20 tools, 3 kanban lifecycle hooks, a dashboard tab and an `duckwork agora` CLI; installing writes nothing — the three bundled skills are deployed by an explicit `duckwork agora setup`. Disclosure — creates a Duckwork profile per worker by asking core to provision it (`duckwork profile create --clone`, which copies config.yaml and .env into the new profile as owner-only files, never symlinks to the real credentials); spawns `duckwork -p <profile> chat -Q -q` subprocesses to speak in discussions and to run dispatched tasks, which execute as full agents with that profile's toolset, including terminal and file writes inside the project workdir. Those subprocesses receive `--yolo --accept-hooks` ONLY when the project opted in via `agora_start_project(allow_unattended=True)`; the default is off, so a freshly installed team can read, discuss and plan but its flagged writes and shell commands fail closed. Also reads and writes the kanban database (tasks, task_comments, task_events, task_runs, task_links) restricted to its own project boards, including a persistent team-channel task pinned in `scheduled` status, and deletes a project's own tasks when it stops or completes; registers one recurring cron job and writes its runner script to DUCKWORK_HOME/scripts/leader_heartbeat.sh; writes AGENTS.md into the configured project workdir; deploys three bundled skills into DUCKWORK_HOME/skills/collaboration/; and serves a dashboard tab plus REST routes through the Duckwork dashboard. No network egress of its own — model calls happen inside the spawned Duckwork subprocesses under the operator's own provider credentials.

No credential, .env or auth.json reads, no network calls, no shell commands, no background processes, no telemetry.

entries.description: Guardrails that follow what a conversation has read. Once a session reads untrusted content (a web page, a browser snapshot, an MCP or third-party plugin's output, a customer's message), airlock seals it: messages to anyone but the owner, network writes, pushes and deploys, memory, skill and cron writes, browser input, URLs that could carry data out and code that reaches the network go through Duckwork's own approval gate. Walls hold in every session: credential paths and secret files, the guard's own files and Duckwork's config, shell startup files, other profiles, commands that switch approvals off. Shell commands are read the way the shell reads them, so a command that computes or hides what it runs (eval, base64 | sh, $G push, wildcards, write-then-run) is refused until written in clear. Subagents inherit the seal. It also catches an injection by its signature: recognized secrets never leave in a call; a private marker in the agent's context locks the session if it shows up in a tool call; a send to an address the untrusted content named is blocked; repeated refusals lock the session; lookalike Unicode in commands is refused. Plugin and MCP tools nobody admitted need approval. Observe mode, stop switch, `duckwork airlock check|demo|log`. Tested on a corpus of 251 attacks and everyday commands, and end to end in the official image. Disclosure — hooks only (pre_tool_call, post_tool_call, pre_llm_call, subagent_start, on_session_reset, post_approval_response), no tools. No network, no LLM call, runs no command. Reads the profile's config.yaml (home channels, approvals mode) and its own policy file (<DUCKWORK_HOME>/airlock.yaml); lists directories to expand wildcards in commands it checks. Writes under plugin-data/airlock: a journal of decisions, taints and approvals that includes tool arguments, truncated (journal.args: none leaves them out), the taint state and the stop switch. When nobody can approve (--yolo, approvals.mode: off, cron set to approve) it blocks instead of letting Duckwork auto-approve (policy approvals_off: follow restores Duckwork's behaviour). Install scan: caution, because the default policy and the shell reader name the patterns airlock guards against (startup files, crontab, credential commands, exfiltration shapes).
known_issues: Built for in-process plugins (Duckwork's default): under plugins.isolation: host it cannot tell third-party plugin tools from Duckwork's own.
